en: Now, when working with Pi, all your work
happens in so-called sessions. Whenever you
run Pi like this, a new session starts.
And inside of Pi, you can start a new
session without quitting it by running /new.
This also starts a new session. A new
session then basically means that you start
fresh with an empty context window. And as
you then work on your tasks and as you work
with Pi,
more and more messages and tool calls and
agent responses and so on get added to that
session.
Now, you can always resume a paused session
by typing
/resume, and that will show you a list of
all your paused sessions per project. So in
this project here, I only have one paused
session, but if I were in a new session
and I were to send a message like, what can
you do for me? Which is kind of pointless,
but a good example,
that is in a new session. So a new message,
a new response, and if I now type you'll see
there are 2 sessions to choose from. And you
can always go back to an older session and
continue from it. And of course, you'll then
start with all the context that belonged to
that session with the entire message
history, all the tool calls, it'll all be
there.
If you already know that you wanna continue
an existing session, you can also start Py
with py
-r for resume, and it will open that session
picker right at the start. So that's a
quicker way of jumping in an older session.
And if you know that you wanna continue your
last session, the last session you worked
in, you can use py -c for continue and it
will also reopen an existing session. In
this case, the last session you actively
interacted with. So you got back a response
or you sent a message to.
Inside of a session, you can also type
/session to get some summary statistics,
some information about that session. You
find information about the file where it's
stored, and I'll get back to that. You'll
find a session ID. You see the number of
messages, tool call results, and so on in
there, and the tokens consumed.
Also the estimated cost of that session,
though don't worry if you are in a
subscription like the ChatGPT subscription.
This is just for information purposes. Of
course, you'll not actually be billed here
because you're in a subscription. But
it's still interesting to see what your
tokens would have cost you normally.
You can also type /name to give your session
a display name, like for example,
first-demo.
So now this session is named first-demo. If
I type /session, I can see that display name
here.
And assigning such a name can be helpful
because if you then resume a session with py
-r or from inside Py with resume, you'll see
that name here, which can of course make it
a bit easier to identify identify a session
you want to continue working in. So that's
why assigning a name could be useful.
If you know that you want to name a session,
you can also run py
--name when you start Py
to assign a name to that session you're
about to start, to the new session you're
about to start. And you can, by the way,
also pick names that contain a whitespace.
You should just wrap them in double quotes
then.
Like another demo.
So now I start a new session. It will have
that name as you see
if you type
/session again.
